author: blu
body: This chapter used to be byte-aligned framing with a Deflate payload -- self consistent, and not RFC 7932 by any reading. Nothing of that survives except the Huffman machinery, which is Deflate's: the same optimal code-length build, the same bit writer and reader, the same canonical decode tables.

author: blu
body: The order the code-length code's own lengths travel in, and the fixed code that carries each of them. Both are the format's, not ours.

author: blu
body: Copy length codes, the same shape. The base starts at TWO, the shortest copy the format can name.

author: blu
body: A cost no real plan can reach, so a plan that cannot be built loses every comparison it is in without needing a second field to say so.

author: blu
body: A thousand and twenty-four is the floor context modelling already uses for the same reason, an extra table only paying on a long block. It is deliberately the same number.

author: blu
body: Reading a symbol back means finding which group it lands in, since the bases are not in order. The group then gives the high three bits of each code and the symbol's own low six bits give the rest.

author: blu
body: THE ALPHABET HAS ELEVEN GROUPS OF SIXTY-FOUR AND THIS MODELLED NINE. The nine in brotli-ic-bases above all start at 128; symbols 0 to 127 were absent entirely, so brotli-ic-group walked off the end of the table and answered zero, and the insert code came out as a negative index into brotli-ins-base. On the prose oracle stream the very first command is symbol 34 and the insert length read back as 8333441927550439407.

author: blu
body: Since every group is exactly sixty-four wide the group is the symbol divided by sixty-four, and no search is needed. The offsets are read off the nine-entry table above, which is oracle-validated, rather than from the RFC's prose.

author: blu
body: A simple prefix code spells its symbols in a fixed width, and the width is the bits needed to count the alphabet. Sixty-four takes six, which is the constant that was written in; five hundred and twenty takes ten.

author: blu
body: The check that settles the width is external. Each stream's original length is known on the host, and a meta-block length field decodes to that length only if every bit before it was consumed correctly, so a candidate width is either right or it is off by three bits and the length is nonsense.

author: blu
body: The window is not decoration. It is half of the rule separating a copy from a dictionary reference, so a reader that assumes sixteen while the stream declares twenty-two turns ordinary copies into dictionary lookups.

author: blu
body: The stream-level and meta-block-level fields the command loop needs, carried as one value rather than as three more parameters on a loop that already takes fourteen. The window comes from WBITS and is fixed for the stream; the postfix and direct fields are read per meta-block.

author: blu
body: A Huffman build can hand back a code longer than the format allows. Clamping alone breaks the Kraft equality, so the excess is repaid by lengthening the shortest codes until the sum fits the tree again.

author: blu
body: THE REPAIR AIMS AT EQUALITY, NOT AT "NO LONGER TOO BIG", AND THAT DISTINCTION WAS A REAL DEFECT. Lengthening a code by one step reduces the Kraft sum by a power of two, so a loop that lengthens the shortest code until the sum is no longer OVER-subscribed can step straight past equality and leave it UNDER- subscribed. An under-subscribed code is incomplete, `brotli-space` rejects it, the caller answers `brotli-code-bad`, and the whole plan is discarded as `brotli-huge` with no diagnostic anywhere -- a silent ratio ceiling that looks exactly like a plan that was honestly outcosted. It cost the static dictionary most of its reach: a command list with about twenty distinct insert-and-copy symbols could not be described at all.

author: blu
body: So each step now picks a symbol whose adjustment FITS the remaining gap rather than the largest one available, and the two directions are symmetric. Over subscribed: lengthen the shortest code whose reduction does not overshoot. Under subscribed: shorten the longest code whose increase does not overshoot. A code at `maxlen` shortened by one step adds exactly one, so the gap can always be closed by ones once nothing coarser fits.

author: blu
body: An alphabet with exactly one symbol in use cannot be made complete by any of this -- one leaf fills half a tree whatever length it is given -- so it never reaches here: `brotli-code-of` answers a simple code naming that symbol, which is the form the format provides for the case.

author: blu
body: Writing a length for every symbol is wasteful once an alphabet is sparse. The insert-and-copy alphabet has 704 symbols and a block uses a few dozen of them, so the description is mostly zeros, one code apiece.

author: blu
body: The item list is built ONCE and then histogrammed, costed and written from. The three used to walk the lengths separately, which is how a writer and a cost function drift apart.

author: blu
body: So the item list is built BOTH ways and the shorter description wins, which is the same arrangement the literal and match encodings already have. Code 16 can then only help.

author: blu
body: A description carries its items, its code-length code, and what the two cost together, so a caller cannot cost one and emit the other.

target: section:A Prefix Code As One Value
author: blu
body: Three codes are written now -- literals, insert-and-copy, distances -- and each is either simple or complex depending on how many symbols it actually uses. That decision, the lengths, the canonical codes and the cost of describing the code all travel together, so a caller cannot cost one shape and emit the other.

author: blu
body: A single-symbol code is held as bk-single with all its LENGTHS ZERO, which is not a placeholder: a simple code naming one symbol costs zero bits to use, so the same emit loop and the same cost sum give the right answer for both shapes without ever asking which they are holding. Only the code's own description differs, and that is what brotli-write-code branches on.

author: blu
body: The choice between stored and compressed is made by counting bits, not by building both. Every term below is exactly what the emitter goes on to write.

author: blu
body: A stored meta-block costs its header, whatever padding takes it to a byte boundary, and the bytes themselves.

author: blu
body: An extra tree costs its whole description, so more trees only pay on a long block. Every candidate is costed against the single-tree plan and the cheaper is emitted, which is what makes this unable to lose.

author: blu
body: THIS READER IGNORED THE CONTEXT MODE FIELD UNTIL 2026-07-19, and that was a correctness bug rather than a missing feature: the field was skipped with the other twelve fixed header bits and every literal was given a mode-zero context, so a stream from any other encoder using mode two decoded to the WRONG BYTES with no error anywhere. Our own encoder writes mode zero, so no round trip could see it, and the interop harness only ever asked whether .NET could read OUR output -- never whether we could read .NET's.

author: blu
body: The mode and its tables travel together, so that the one function both halves compute a context with cannot be given one without the other. An encoder and a decoder that disagree here produce a stream that decodes to plausible garbage rather than one that is refused, which is the worst failure shape available.

author: blu
body: The symbols are written in order, so a value's canonical code equals the value and the decoder can read the map as fixed-width fields.

author: blu
body: A context costs what its bytes cost under a cluster's lengths. A symbol the cluster has no code for is charged a flat miss rather than treated as free: the assignment that follows rebuilds every cluster from what was assigned to it, so the final codes always cover their own members and the miss only ever steers the choice.

author: blu
body: NOTHING RE-SEEDS AN ABANDONED CLUSTER. The assignment is free to route every context to the same cluster while the description is still charged for k trees, so a collapsed plan cannot beat the single-tree plan it is costed against. A re-seed was written, measured, and TAKEN BACK OUT, because on this corpus it moved not one byte: see the paragraph on what the literal plan is actually worth, below.

author: blu
body: A literal plan: how many trees, which context takes which, and the trees. One tree is the shape this chapter emitted before, and it costs the single NTREESL bit it always did, so a region that declines context modelling is byte-identical to what it was.

author: blu
body: The single-tree plan is always built. Two and four trees are tried only on a region long enough to have a chance of paying for them, and the winner is whichever costs fewest bits once its own description is counted.

author: blu
body: Insert-and-copy first, because it is the clean half: literal block types multiply the context map (the tree is context-map[type * 64 + context]) and distance types would want their own map, while insert-and-copy has neither.

author: blu
body: Both of these codes are SIMPLE ones, for the reason the context map's is: with two blocks the alphabets are tiny and evenly used, and a flat alphabet cannot be described by the complex form at all.

author: blu
body: Two blocks, cut at one command. The first block's length rides in the header and the second's arrives at the boundary, so exactly one switch is written and the meta-block ends when the second block's count runs out.

author: blu
body: Only the insert-and-copy symbols differ between candidates -- the literals, the distances and every extra-bit field are the same whichever way the commands are cut -- so the comparison counts those and each candidate's own description, and nothing else. Three cuts are tried and the single-block plan is one of the candidates, so splitting cannot lose.

author: blu
body: Distance block types, the same shape as the insert-and-copy ones with two differences that decide the whole design.

author: blu
body: The cut is named by a COMMAND index so the emitter can test for it directly, and it is chosen by walking to the command that carries the wanted distance. That guarantees the boundary lands on a command that actually writes one.

author: blu
body: The two bits in the off case are NBLTYPESD and NTREESD, both of which used to sit in the emitter's fixed header count. They move here because neither is one bit any more once splitting is possible, the same way the literal tree count moved into the literal plan and the insert-and-copy count into the split.

author: blu
body: A second distance code has to pay for its own description, a context map and a block-type switch before it returns anything, so it is only tried where there are enough distances for that to be possible. The single-block plan is one of the candidates, so splitting cannot lose.

author: blu
body: The literal code is built once and used three times: to decide, to describe itself, and to code the literals.

author: blu
body: A command is some literals to insert and then a copy of something already written. The matcher is Lz77's, the same one Deflate uses, so the tokens come back as literals and matches and a command is just a run of literals terminated by one match.

author: blu
body: The LAST command may have no copy at all. That is the trick the literals-only block was already built on and it still holds: the decoder inserts the literals, checks whether it has produced the meta-block length, and only THEN reads a distance. So a trailing run of literals needs no match to close it, and a block with no matches anywhere is simply the case where there is one command and it is that one. Literals-only stopped being a separate encoder here -- it is a command list of length one.

author: blu
body: How many literal tokens run unbroken from here, capped at the longest word the corpus holds. A dictionary word may only replace LITERALS: the matcher's own matches are left alone, so taking a word can never cost a match that was already found, and the walk never has to take a token apart.

author: blu
body: The matcher's command list again, with dictionary words taken where the corpus has one. It is built as a THIRD candidate rather than as an improvement to the second, so the dictionary is costed against not using it and cannot make any input larger. Where no word is found anywhere, this list is identical to the matcher's and the two cost the same.

author: blu
body: Which lookup a plan uses is the plan's own business: the same walk serves both, so the dictionary can be costed with transforms and without.

author: blu
body: A RANGE WALK IS THE REASON IT CANNOT BE COMPUTED IN PLACE. Block splitting costs sub-ranges of the command list, and the code for the command at index i depends on every distance before it. A walk starting at i does not know the state at i. One pass from the beginning does, so one pass is what runs.

author: blu
body: A distance no copy can carry, so the first command in a meta-block never matches it and never takes the shorthand.

author: blu
body: The cost of a command list, counted in the same order the emitter writes it. The fixed thirty-three bits are the meta-block header and the block-type, postfix, context and tree-count fields.

author: blu
body: The fixed twenty-nine bits are the meta-block header and the postfix, direct, context-mode and literal-block-type fields. Four counts are NOT among them, because none of them is one bit any more: the literal tree count travels inside the literal plan's description, the insert-and-copy block type count inside the split's, and the distance block type and distance tree counts inside the distance split's, each carrying whatever machinery it turns on.

author: blu
body: The two candidates are costed the same way because they ARE the same encoder, differing only in their command list: one command that inserts everything, or the matcher's. Whichever counts fewer bits is emitted, and a stored block wins over both when neither pays for itself.

author: blu
body: Three plans now, costed the same way because they ARE the same encoder differing only in their command list: one command inserting everything, the matcher's, and the matcher's with dictionary words taken where the corpus has one. Whichever counts fewest bits is emitted, and a stored block wins over all three when none pays for itself.

author: blu
body: Building the three codes is the expensive half of costing a plan, so the cost and the emission build them the same way from the same command list rather than sharing a cached copy: the plan is the only thing carried between them, and two readings of it cannot disagree.

author: blu
body: The reader mirrors the writer. It handles the subset this chapter emits -- one block type of each kind, context mode zero with up to four literal trees, and no distance context map -- which is what our own round-trip needs; the interop harness is what proves the OUTPUT is valid for a general decoder.

author: blu
body: This is only sound because the corpus is immutable and identical every time it is loaded, so which reference happens to be first cannot change the answer.

author: blu
body: THE DISTANCE RING BUFFER BELONGS TO THE STREAM, NOT TO THE META-BLOCK, and this reader re-initialised it per meta-block until it was measured. Everything else a meta-block header carries is genuinely per-meta-block -- the prefix codes, the context maps, the block-type state, the postfix and direct fields -- so putting the cache beside them looked right and read right.

author: blu
body: Thirteen bits of the compressed header carry three block-type counts, the postfix and direct-distance fields, one context mode and two tree counts. All but the context mode are skipped rather than checked, which is what limits the reader to our own subset.

author: blu
body: The tables cost a load, so they are built only when the mode actually asks for them; a mode-zero stream pays nothing, the same arrangement the dictionary has.

author: blu
body: Then the three prefix codes in the format's order -- literals, insert-and-copy, distances -- and then commands until the meta-block length is met.

author: blu
body: A prefix code is read the way it was written: two bits of HSKIP say simple or complex, and a simple code here always names exactly one symbol, because that is the only simple code this chapter emits. Reading it back as a single symbol that costs no bits is what lets one command loop serve every block the encoder produces, including the all-one-byte region that used to need its own reader.

author: blu
body: THE BLOCK-TYPE AND BLOCK-COUNT CODES ARE ORDINARY PREFIX CODES and this read them as simple ones only, through a decoder that also got the four-symbol tree-select case wrong. Our encoder emits simple codes here, so nothing round-tripping our own output could see either fault.

author: blu
body: The distance side's whole state travels as one record rather than as five more parameters on a loop that already carries fourteen: the block machinery, the current type and what is left of its block, the codes, and the context map that chooses between them.

author: blu
body: The header is read a category at a time, because that is how it is written: each block-type count carries its own two codes and its first block length before the next category begins.

author: blu
body: The distance alphabet size follows from both fields, so it is computed here and handed to the code reader instead of the sixty-four that only the zero case has.

author: blu
body: The word id is what is left after subtracting that maximum, and it carries a transform in its high part: id divided by the count of words at this length. Our encoder emits transform ZERO only, so this reads transform zero only, and takes the word modulo the count. That is the same subsetting as the rest of this reader -- and the interop harness is what proves the OUTPUT is valid for a general decoder. A stream from elsewhere using a transform will decode to the untransformed word here.

author: blu
body: The word under one transform type. The omit types can empty a word entirely, which is legal and produces nothing at all between the prefix and the suffix.

author: blu
body: The seam is where the format's own is. The loop reads the command header, the literal half consumes the insert, and the distance half resolves the copy.

author: blu
body: The distance itself is code zero, the most recent one, which the cache already answers and deliberately does not disturb.

author: blu
body: Reading a complex prefix code: the code-length code first, then the code lengths themselves, each stopping when its tree is full.

author: blu
body: `rep` carries the count standing and `lastc` which repeat code produced it, so a different code, or any ordinary length, resets both.

author: blu
body: THIS USED TO REQUIRE THE FIRST BIT TO BE THE ZERO OUR OWN ENCODER WRITES, which made it a test for our own output rather than for the format. Every stream from every other encoder was refused here, before a single field was read, and the refusal was indistinguishable from an empty input. The window field is variable width and its legal range is ten through twenty-four, so a value outside that is the only thing this can honestly reject.
